# Choice of statistical test

If you've been in a statistical methods course, you may remember that there were many methods presented. How do we know which one to pick?

For a relatively simple randomized clinical trial with

- 2 treatment arms
- Participants are independent
- Primary endpoint at 1 timepoint, either (approximately) continuous or binary

we have the following options:

| **type of outcome** | **effect estimate** | **not adjusted** | **adjusted** |
|------------------|------------------|------------------|------------------|
| **continuous** \* | mean difference | $t$-test | linear regression |
| **binary** (yes / no) | odds ratio | $\chi$-square test | logistic regression |
| ... | ... | ... | ... |

::: {.callout-important}
Continuous outcomes usually need to be only approximately normally distributed! Even where a method make "assume normality", as in say the t-test, "it is not in fact necessary for the distribution of the observed data to be normal, but rather the sample values should be compatible with the population (which they represent) having a normal distribution" [@normal]. A good example of an outcome which is most certainly not normally distributed is length of stay in the hospital
:::


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true"}
library(tidyverse)
theme_set(theme_bw(base_size = 12))
set.seed(20261026)
ex <- tibble(x = 1:200,
             los = round(rexp(200, 1/10)))

ggplot(aes(los), data = ex) +
  geom_histogram() +
  xlab("length of stay in hospital (days)") + ylab("number of observations")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![length of stay as a common example of an outcome that is definitely not normally distributed.](choice_files/figure-html/lengthofstay-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::



Selection of statistical methods is however usually more complicated than this! For example, we have not considered outcomes that are rates or survival times, more than 2 groups, clustered outcomes (either from cluster randomized trials or repeated measures from longitudinal studies), or crossover trials.

For more information on selection of statistical methods, see e.g. Chapter 34 in @kirkwood (especially Table 34.3). A competent statistician should be on your study team, and can help you determine the most appropriate design and methods for your study.

If you need help finding a statistician at UZH, contact the [Clinical Research Methods](https://www.ebpi.uzh.ch/en/research_methods/methodsexpertise.html) group at the EBPI, or see this list from the [UZH Math](https://www.math.uzh.ch/consulting/general) department.
